Introduction to surveymixr

Siyang Ni

2025-11-13

Source: vignettes/surveymixr-intro.Rmd
surveymixr-intro.Rmd

Introduction

What is surveymixr?

surveymixr implements growth mixture modeling (GMM) for longitudinal data with full integration of complex survey design features. This is the first R package to combine mixture models with stratification, clustering, and probability weights—a feature set previously only available in proprietary software like Mplus.

Why surveymixr?

Growth mixture models are essential for studying heterogeneous developmental trajectories in fields like criminology, sociology, and psychology. However, analyzing data from complex surveys (e.g., Millennium Cohort Study, Add Health, NLSY) requires proper handling of survey design features. Existing R packages have critical limitations:

Feature surveymixr lcmm flexmix lavaan
Growth mixture models ✓ ✓ Partial ✗
Stratification ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗
Clustering (PSUs) ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗
Probability weights ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗
Sandwich SEs ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗
BLRT ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗
R3STEP ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗
1000+ random starts ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗

Key Features

  • Complex Survey Integration: Proper handling of stratification, clustering, and weights
  • Bootstrap Likelihood Ratio Test (BLRT): Gold standard for class enumeration
  • R3STEP Analysis: Classification uncertainty correction for auxiliary variables
  • Extensive Diagnostics: Convergence tracking, entropy, classification quality
  • Multiple Random Starts: Parallel processing of 500-1000+ starts
  • Publication-Ready Plots: Professional trajectory visualization

Installation 

# From CRAN (once published)
install.packages("surveymixr")

# Development version from GitHub
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("siyangni/surveymixr")

Quick Start

Let’s analyze self-control trajectories from our simulated Millennium Cohort Study data:

library(surveymixr)

# Load example data
data(mcs_simulated)

# Preview data structure
head(mcs_simulated)
#>   id age selfcontrol true_class stratum cluster weight
#>   1   3        8.23          1       1      45   1.23
#>   1   5        8.45          1       1      45   1.23
#>   1   7        8.67          1       1      45   1.23
#>   ...

Fit a 3-Class Model 

fit <- gmm_survey(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id",
  time = "age",
  outcome = "selfcontrol",
  n_classes = 3,
  growth_model = "linear",
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "cluster",
  weights = "weight",
  starts = 500,
  cores = 4,
  verbose = TRUE
)

View Results 

summary(fit)

Key Output Sections:

  1. Growth Parameters: Class-specific intercepts and slopes with survey-adjusted SEs
  2. Class Proportions: Weighted (population) vs unweighted (sample) estimates
  3. Fit Indices: BIC, entropy, classification quality
  4. Convergence: Random starts diagnostics

Visualize Trajectories 

plot(fit, type = "trajectories")

This creates a publication-ready plot showing: - Class-specific trajectory lines - 95% confidence intervals - Class proportions in legend - Entropy in subtitle

Model Selection

Determining the optimal number of classes is critical. Use gmm_select() to compare multiple solutions:

selection <- gmm_select(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id",
  time = "age",
  outcome = "selfcontrol",
  classes = 1:5,
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "cluster",
  weights = "weight",
  criteria = c("BIC", "BLRT", "entropy"),
  blrt_samples = 100,
  starts = 200,
  cores = 4
)

print(selection)

Interpreting Results:

Criterion What it Measures Decision Rule
BIC Model parsimony Lower is better
Entropy Classification certainty Higher is better (>0.8 ideal)
BLRT K vs K-1 comparison p < 0.05 favors K classes

The BLRT is considered the gold standard. A significant BLRT (p < 0.05) indicates that K classes fit better than K-1 classes. Continue testing until BLRT is non-significant.

Visualize Model Selection 

plot_model_selection(selection)

Adding Covariates: R3STEP Analysis

When relating class membership to auxiliary variables (e.g., delinquency, academic achievement), the naive “classify-analyze” approach produces biased estimates. The R3STEP method corrects for classification uncertainty:

# Analyze distal outcomes
r3step_results <- r3step(
  gmm_object = fit,
  distal_vars = c("delinquency", "academic_achievement"),
  data = mcs_simulated[!duplicated(mcs_simulated$id), ],  # One row per person
  method = "BCH"
)

summary(r3step_results)

R3STEP Output:

  • Class means for each auxiliary variable (corrected for classification error)
  • Survey-adjusted SEs
  • Omnibus tests (any class differences?)
  • Pairwise comparisons (which classes differ?)
  • Effect sizes (Cohen’s d)

Survey Design Considerations

When to Use Survey Features

Use survey weights when: - Data come from a probability sample with unequal selection probabilities - You want population-representative estimates - Different groups were oversampled

Use clustering when: - Individuals are nested within units (schools, neighborhoods, PSUs) - Observations within clusters are correlated - This is common in national cohort studies

Use stratification when: - Population was divided into strata before sampling - Sampling rates differ across strata - Example: geographic regions, urban/rural

Weighted vs Unweighted Results 

# Compare weighted and unweighted class proportions
class_proportions(fit, weighted = TRUE)
class_proportions(fit, weighted = FALSE)

Differences indicate that: 1. Sampling was not proportional to population 2. Weights are adjusting for over/under-sampling 3. Weighted estimates are more population-representative

Convergence Diagnostics

Multiple random starts are essential because mixture models often have local maxima:

diagnostics <- diagnose_convergence(fit)
print(diagnostics)

What to Look For:

  • Best solution replicated: Should occur 2+ times
  • Distinct local maxima: Few (< 3-5) is good; many suggests instability
  • Convergence rate: Most starts should converge

If problems detected:

# Increase random starts
fit_more <- gmm_survey(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id",
  time = "age",
  outcome = "selfcontrol",
  n_classes = 3,
  starts = 1000,  # Increase from 500
  cores = 4
)

Classification Quality

Assess how well individuals are classified:

qual <- classification_quality(fit)
print(qual)

Key Metrics:

  • Entropy: 0-1 scale (>0.8 excellent, 0.6-0.8 good, <0.6 poor)
  • AvePP: Average posterior probability for assigned class (>0.9 ideal)
  • OCC: Odds of correct classification (>5 desirable)

If classification is poor:

  1. Consider fewer classes
  2. Try different growth model specification
  3. Add time-varying covariates
  4. Check for data quality issues

Growth Model Specifications

surveymixr supports multiple growth models:

Linear Growth (Default) 

fit_linear <- gmm_survey(..., growth_model = "linear")

Model: yit=β0k+β1k⋅t+ϵity_{it} = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k} \cdot t + \epsilon_{it}

Quadratic Growth 

fit_quad <- gmm_survey(..., growth_model = "quadratic")

Model: yit=β0k+β1k⋅t+β2k⋅t2+ϵity_{it} = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k} \cdot t + \beta_{2k} \cdot t^2 + \epsilon_{it}

Useful for: - Non-linear trajectories - Developmental curves with acceleration/deceleration

Free Time Scores 

fit_free <- gmm_survey(..., growth_model = "free_basis")

Estimates time scores rather than fixing them. Useful when: - Time intervals are irregular - Developmental time is not linear with chronological time

Comparison with Mplus

For researchers familiar with Mplus, surveymixr provides similar functionality with some key differences:

Syntax Comparison

Mplus:

VARIABLE:
  CLASSES = c(3);
  CLUSTER = psu;
  STRATIFICATION = stratum;
  WEIGHT = weight;

ANALYSIS:
  TYPE = MIXTURE;
  STARTS = 500 100;

MODEL:
  %OVERALL%
  i s | y@0 y@1 y@2 y@3;

surveymixr:

gmm_survey(
  data = data,
  outcome = "y",
  n_classes = 3,
  cluster = "psu",
  strata = "stratum",
  weights = "weight",
  starts = 500
)

Conversion Utilities 

# Convert Mplus input to surveymixr code
r_code <- mplus_to_surveymixr("model.inp")
cat(r_code)

# Export surveymixr results in Mplus format
surveymixr_to_mplus(fit, file = "results.txt")

Advanced Topics

Missing Data

surveymixr uses Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) by default:

  • MCAR: Missing completely at random
  • MAR: Missing at random (conditional on observed data)
  • MNAR: Not recommended; requires specialized models

Pattern of missingness is automatically handled. No need for imputation.

Parallelization

For large datasets or many starts, use parallel processing:

# Check available cores
parallel::detectCores()

# Use multiple cores
fit <- gmm_survey(..., starts = 1000, cores = 8)

Benefits: - 1000 starts in ~5-10 minutes (vs hours sequentially) - Linear speedup with cores - Essential for BLRT

Best Practices

Sample Size Requirements

Minimum recommendations:

  • Per class: At least 50-100 individuals
  • Smallest class: Should be >5% of sample
  • Time points: At least 3 (4-6 better)
  • For BLRT: Larger samples (N > 500) better

Model Building Strategy

  1. Start simple: Fit 1-5 class models with linear growth
  2. Use model selection: Compare BIC, entropy, BLRT
  3. Check convergence: Ensure best solution replicated
  4. Assess quality: Examine classification metrics
  5. Add complexity: Try quadratic growth if justified
  6. Interpret substantively: Classes must make theoretical sense
  7. Validate: R3STEP with auxiliary variables

Reporting Results

A complete analysis report should include:

  1. Sample description: N, time points, missing data rate
  2. Model selection: Table with fit indices for 1-5 classes
  3. Final model: Parameter estimates with SEs (table)
  4. Trajectory plot: Publication-quality figure
  5. Classification: Entropy, class sizes, AvePP
  6. Convergence: Random starts, replications
  7. Survey design: Weights, clustering, stratification details
  8. R3STEP: Auxiliary variable analyses (if applicable)

Getting Help

Documentation

# Vignettes
browseVignettes("surveymixr")

Common Issues

“Best solution not replicated” → Increase starts to 1000+

“Poor entropy (<0.6)” → Try fewer classes or different growth model

“Very small class (<5%)” → May not be substantively meaningful; consider K-1 classes

“Long computation time” → Use cores for parallelization; reduce starts for initial exploration
